title: South Korea Passes $1 Trillion in Exports, Fourth Country Ever, on AI Chip Boom
excerpt: A one-year leap from last year's $709 billion record, powered by Samsung and SK hynix memory sales into the AI data-centre build-out.
body:
• South Korea's exports for 2026 passed $1 trillion on Thursday, making it the fourth country ever to reach the mark, after China, the United States and Germany.
  • The milestone took a single year from last year's record $709.3 billion — a leap the other members needed two to six years to make.
  • Semiconductors did the heavy lifting: chip exports rose 196.9% to $413.4 billion from January 1 to November 10, 42.9% of all exports, per customs figures reported by Aju Press.
  • For investors, the concentration is the story: chips generated about three-quarters of the export increase, and the Korea Development Institute expects real export growth to slow from 10.3% this year to 8.1% next year.

South Korea's exports so far this year have exceeded $1 trillion, driven by the global AI chip boom, making it the fourth country in the world to reach the milestone after Germany, the United States and China, Reuters reported. Exports passed the mark as of 0509 GMT on Thursday, the trade ministry said — 2:09 p.m. in Seoul, according to preliminary data from the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources and the Korea Customs Service reported by Aju Press. It is the club's first new entrant in 19 years: the United States and Germany crossed in 2006 and China in 2007.

The fastest climb in the club's history

The speed is what sets Korea apart. Its exports stood at $709.3 billion last year, a record it surpassed by September 5 this year; the other members took two to six years to travel from $700 billion to $1 trillion, by Aju Press's calculations from WTO and national data. Korea did it in one. The longer arc runs from $19 million of exports in 1948 — dried fish and agar to Hong Kong and Macau — through $100 million in 1964, a date still marked as Trade Day, to $100 billion in 1995 and $500 billion in 2011. Semiconductors first became the top export in 1992.

Chips, and the AI build-out around them

Samsung Electronics and SK hynix supply the high-bandwidth memory, server DRAM and NAND flash that AI data centres consume, and both described rising data-centre demand in their third-quarter reports — Samsung citing strong server demand pushing memory prices up amid capacity constraints, SK hynix reporting expanding sales of server DDR5, HBM4 and enterprise solid-state drives. The same build-out lifted adjacent lines: computer exports jumped nearly sixfold to $5.85 billion in October, led by server solid-state drives, and shipments of electrical equipment such as transformers and cables for data centres rose 74% to a monthly record of $1.99 billion. Cosmetics exports set their own record at $12.57 billion for January to October. Car exports were the exception, slipping 1.7% to $58.6 billion over the same period as US tariffs and overseas production weighed.

"Now, we need to turn this achievement into sustainable growth. We will enhance the competitiveness of major industries and grow future growth engines, such as AI and bio."

— President Lee Jae Myung, in a post on X, via Reuters

The Lee administration plans a 162.3 trillion won ($121.94 billion) Future Response Fund to channel excess tax revenue from the chip boom toward growth industries, young people, regional development and education, Reuters reported. Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan, visiting Incheon New Port on November 17, credited businesses that opened overseas markets and the workers and logistics staff who moved Korean products around the world.

The concentration problem

Two cautions sit under the headline. The first is breadth: Reuters noted that domestic demand remains weak and the benefits of the export boom have yet to trickle down to many households, with consumer sentiment hurt by high interest rates and prices. The second is composition. Aju Press's reading of the Bank of Korea's trade indices shows October export values up 107.6% year on year against volumes up 43.9% — meaning a large share of the surge is higher prices, above all for memory, rather than more goods shipped. A Bank of Korea forecasting official said on November 10 that chip prices were unlikely to keep rising at their current pace even if AI investment continues.

What to watch

Korea's finance minister said last month that economic growth is expected to quicken to the mid-3% range this year on record chip exports, after expanding 1% last year. Whether the trillion-dollar level is a floor or a peak depends on how long memory prices hold and how much more demand Samsung and SK hynix can supply — the same AI-spending question that now runs through the earnings of every chipmaker selling into the data-centre build-out.
